en: Padamañjarī.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
To the Victor who has reached the further shore of the ocean of etymological analysis...
Having bowed three times to the pure Dhamma and the unsurpassed Saṅgha, I, Padumañjarī,
compose this work for the growth of the intellect of those with immature understanding.
Now, the word *buddha*, a masculine noun ending in the vowel *a*, is explained.
The Buddha taught the Dhamma to gods and humans;
the Buddhas taught the Dhamma to gods and humans.
O Buddha, you indeed protect me;
O Buddhas, you too protect me.
I reverently pay homage to the Blessed Buddha.
We pay full homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One;
the Dhamma is taught by the Buddha, the Blessed One;
the Dhamma has been taught by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
The Blessed Buddha causes the great multitude to practice well;
through the Blessed Buddhas, people go to the auspicious state;
one offers flowers to the Blessed Buddha.
One offers flowers to the Blessed Buddhas;
may one obtain the state of peace through the Blessed Buddhas;
from the Blessed Buddhas, radiance streams forth.
What could the supernatural power of the Buddha, the Blessed One, not accomplish?
Through the miracles of psychic power performed by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
the great multitude gains confidence in the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
The mind is established upon the Blessed Buddhas.
Thus ends the first reading.
Now, the word *atta* is stated as a masculine noun ending in *-a*.
The self encounters the suffering of saṃsāra;
the self experiences its own pleasure and pain.
O self, you experience pleasure and pain.
O, experience your own pleasure and pain!
The Buddha, the Blessed One, sees himself;
the Perfectly Enlightened One sees himself.
One experiences pleasure and pain by oneself;
one experiences the fruit of one's own karma by oneself;
there is no such thing as the happiness of saṃsāra belonging to another.
There is no such thing as happiness in existence for oneself;
one's own self alone should be one's refuge.
One's own karma alone should be one's refuge.
Great fear arises from oneself;
great fears are born from oneself;
one's own parents come to be.
The five destinies belong to the self;
disease carries away all strength within the self;
diseases carry away all strength from within the selves.
Thus ends the second reading.
Now the masculine noun *rāja*, ending in the vowel *a*, is discussed.
A king also satisfies the great multitude.
Kings please the great multitude:
"O King, protect the great multitude!
O Kings, protect the great multitude!"
The great multitude sees the king;
the great multitude is seen by the kings;
a great palace is being built for the king.
Great monasteries were caused to be built by kings;
by the king, the great multitude lives in happiness;
by the kings, the great multitude lives in happiness.
The great multitude gives a gift to the king;
the great multitude gives gifts to the ministers;
a great fear arises for the king.
Great fears arise for kings;
there is the king’s auspicious plowing ceremony;
and there are all the royal ornaments.
The great multitude has faith in the king;
the great multitude has faith in kings.
Thus is the third reading.
The word *guṇavat* is called a masculine noun ending in the vowel *a*.
A man possessing virtues has gone to the beautiful Nibbāna;
men possessing virtues have gone to the beautiful Nibbāna.
"O virtuous man, you too should give a gift.
"O virtuous men, you all should give gifts.
"The teacher instructs the virtuous man in the Dhamma."
The teacher teaches the Dhamma to virtuous men;
a monastery was caused to be built by a virtuous man;
monasteries were caused to be built by virtuous men.
The world fares well through a person of virtue;
the worlds fare well through persons of virtue;
the world pays honor to a person of virtue.
People show honor to virtuous persons;
no fear arises from a virtuous person,
nor do fears arise from virtuous persons.
The fame of a virtuous person rises up like a limb;
there is a proclamation of the virtues of virtuous persons;
I delight in a virtuous person even when he is dead.
A virtuous person places his confidence in men who possess good qualities.
Thus ends the fourth lesson.
Now, the word *gacchanto*, a masculine noun ending in the vowel *a*, is being explained.
While walking, Yaññadatta causes a man to carry a burden.
While walking, the Yaññadattas cause a man to perform work.
O, walking Yaññadatta, you protect me!
O, protect me, Yajñadatta, as you go!
The twice-born man asks for a blanket from Yajñadatta as he goes;
the twice-born man asks for a blanket from Yajñadatta while he is going.
While Yaññadatta was going, he gathered flowers from the tree;
while the Yaññadattas were going, they gathered flowers from the tree;
while Yaññadatta was going, someone knew the way.
When the Yaññadattas are going, some know the path;
when Yaññadatta is going, they hold his parasol;
when the Yaññadattas are going, they hold their parasols.
Fear does not arise for Yaññadatta as he goes;
fears do not arise for the Yaññadattas as they go;
an umbrella belongs to Yaññadatta as he goes.
The ornaments belong to the Yajñadattas who are going;
someone has faith in the Yajñadatta who is going;
some have faith in the Yajñadattas who are going.
Thus ends the fifth lesson.
The masculine noun ending in *i*, the word *aggi* (fire), is now discussed.
Furthermore, fire turns wood into charcoal.
They turn wood into fire and embers, saying:
"O fire, dispel the cold! O fires, dispel the cold!"
Whoever extinguishes a fire;
whosoever extinguish fires;
no form whatsoever was burnt by the fire.
Some houses are burnt by fires;
fire burns some houses; fires burn some houses.
The brahmin gives fuel to the fire;
the brahmins give fuel to the fires;
by means of the fire, the smoke constantly departs.
From fires, smoke constantly rises;
there is light from fire,
and there is even light from many fires.
"Whoever has faith in the fire;
whoever among those [deities] has faith in the fires.
Thus is the sixth recitation.
The word *ādi* (beginning) is called a masculine noun ending in the vowel *i*.
"The beginning is bound by a complete Saṅgha";
"the beginnings are bound by the complete monks."
"Venerable sirs, you should perform this for a long time;
venerable sirs, you should carry it out for a long time.
A united Saṅgha sees the beginning."
The bhikkhu sees the beginning, and the Saṅgha [sees] the beginning;
indeed, one exists by means of what is pure at the beginning,
and indeed, one exists by means of those things that are pure at the beginning.
The entire Saṅgha conducts itself well through its leaders;
through its leaders, the Bhikkhu Saṅgha conducts itself well;
someone gives requisites to the leaders.
Some give requisites at the beginning;
with the beginning, the Saṅgha departs;
with the beginnings, the community of monks departs.
Furthermore, it is beneficial to the beginning;
it is beneficial even to those at the beginning;
and the Saṅgha sits together in harmony at the beginning.
First, the community of monks also sits down.
Thus ends the seventh lesson.
Now, the masculine noun *daṇḍin* ending in long *ī* is discussed.
Let even the man with a staff cast away his staff;
let the men with staves cast away their staves;
O man with a staff, cast away your staff!
"O men with staves, cast away the staff!
It is the man with the staff who causes the man to perform the work;
it is the men with staves who cause the men to perform the work."
Let the staff be discarded by the man with the staff;
let the staves be discarded by the men with staves;
the man stands by means of the man with the staff.
Men stand with staffs;
the mind of a man with a staff does not please,
nor does the mind of men with staffs please.
Fear arises from a man with a staff; fears arise from men with staves;
there is the possession of a man with a staff.
Women are the possession of men who carry staves;
the mind does not delight in a man who carries a staff;
and some have no confidence in men who carry staves.
Thus ends the eighth lesson.
Now the masculine noun *bhikkhu*, ending in *u*, is explained.
The monk speaks the Dhamma to the great kings.
The bhikkhus were preaching the Dhamma to the great kings:
"O bhikkhu, teach the sublime Dhamma!
O bhikkhus, teach the sublime Dhamma!"
I bow respectfully to the bhikkhu;
we all bow respectfully to the bhikkhu,
for by the bhikkhu the true Dhamma is taught.
The true Dhamma is well-taught by the bhikkhus;
through the bhikkhus, the world goes to heaven;
through the bhikkhus, the great masses will attain heaven.
A true person gives a gift to a bhikkhu;
true persons give gifts to bhikkhus;
through a bhikkhu, one may attain heaven.
Through the monks, virtuous persons may attain heaven;
there is the bowl and robe of a single monk,
and there are the bowls and robes of many monks.
My mind delights in the bhikkhus;
the virtuous person who has faith finds confidence in the bhikkhus.
Thus is the ninth lesson.
The word *jantu* is said to be a masculine noun ending in the vowel *u*.
*Jantu devadattaṃ kaṭaṃ kārāpeti* (The man causes Devadatta to have the mat made).
*Jantuno devadatte kaṭe kārāpenti* (They cause the man to have the mat made for Devadatta).
"O people, you too should have Devadatta make a mat.
"O people, have Devadatta make a mat for the person.
"I am having this person make a mat; [or] by that very person, on the mat..."
A person has a hut made by a creature, or he causes a dwelling or a hut to be made by that very same creature;
a person has a dwelling or a hut caused to be made by creatures.
Whatever person attains happiness through a noble being,
or whatever beings attain happiness through noble beings—
the wealthy give the wealth of the noble one to those beings.
The wealthy give wealth to those beings who are noble;
whoever is not a noble being among beings disappears,
and whoever are not noble beings disappear from among the noble beings.
The ripening of the fruit belongs to all beings;
for all beings there are the five destinies;
whoever has faith in a noble being, [for that person too there is the ripening of the fruit].
Among noble beings, those who have faith in anyone whatsoever.
Thus ends the tenth lesson.
Now, the word *satthu* (teacher) in the masculine gender ending in *-u* is explained.
The Teacher gave a Dhamma teaching to gods and humans;
the Teachers gave Dhamma teachings to gods and humans.
O Teacher, may you protect the world together with its devas!
O teachers, protect the world together with its devas!
Paying homage with reverence to the Teacher, the King of Dhamma—
may we pay homage with reverence to the Teacher, the King of Dhamma.
By the Teacher, the King of Dharma, the world is awakened to peace;
by the Teachers, the Kings of Dharma, the world is awakened to peace;
through the Teacher, the King of Dharma, one goes to the deathless state.
May the world attain the deathless state through the Teachers, the Kings of Dhamma;
the world offers flowers to the Teacher, the King of Dhamma;
the world offers flowers to the Teachers, the Kings of Dhamma.
The teachers of other sects are defeated by the Teacher, the King of Dhamma;
from the Teachers, the Kings of Dhamma, rays of light stream forth.
I bow down at the feet of the Teacher, the King of Dhamma.
I bow my head at the feet of the Teachers, the Kings of Dhamma.
Who would not cultivate devotion toward the Teacher, the King of Dhamma?
May there be devotion toward the Teachers, the Kings of Dhamma, in birth after birth.
Thus ends the eleventh lesson.
Now the masculine noun *nanta* ending in *u* is explained.
He causes his grandfather to eat that food.
The grandchildren feed their grandfather food, saying:
"O grandson, you too should learn a craft;
O grandchildren, you all should learn crafts."
The teacher teaches the craft to the pupil;
the teachers teach the crafts to the pupils;
by the pupils the flowers are gathered from the tree.
Because of the nephews, the tree was stripped of its flowers;
because of the nephews, the grandfather became happy;
because of the nephews, the great-grandfather became happy.
The grandfather gives the field and land to his grandsons;
the grandfathers give the field and land to their grandsons;
the grandfather has passed away from the grandsons.
The grandfather is separated from his grandson’s clothes and ornaments,
yet he possesses clothes and ornaments himself;
however, the clothes and ornaments belong to the grandchildren.
"Among grandsons, whoever does not have faith;
among grandsons, whichever ones do not have faith.
Thus ends the twelfth lesson.
The masculine word *pitā* ending in the vowel *u* is thus called.
"The father also feeds food to his son" (*pitā pi puttaṃ bhojanaṃ bhojayati*);
"the fathers feed food to their sons" (*pitaro putte bhojanaṃ bhojayanti*).
O father, you too should feed those who have supported you;
O fathers, you should feed them.
A son supports his father with proper care.
Sons support their father with due care;
the father causes his son to perform wholesome deeds;
by the fathers, the son is caused to perform wholesome deeds.
Even a son attains happiness through his father;
sisters attain happiness through their fathers;
a son offers food and drink to his father.
Sons give food and drink to their parents;
when the father has passed away,
the son pays homage at his father’s feet.
Sons pay homage at the feet of their fathers;
a son finds confidence in his father,
and a devoted son finds confidence in his parents.
Thus ends the thirteenth lesson.
Now the masculine noun *bhātṛ*, ending in the vowel *u*, is explained.
A brother causes his sister to perform what is wholesome.
The brothers and sister perform wholesome deeds;
"O brother, you too should perform wholesome deeds";
"O brothers, you all should perform wholesome deeds."
The elder brother causes the work to be done by the younger brother;
the elder brothers cause the work to be done by the younger brothers;
by the younger brothers, the Saṅgha is fed with a meal.
The Saṅgha was fed by the brothers;
through the brothers, the sisters also attain happiness;
through the brothers, the sisters attain happiness.
The elder brother gives clothing to his brother;
the elder brothers give clothing to their brothers;
when the brothers have disappeared, so too does the sister.
The sisters disappear before their brothers;
however, the fields and lands belonging to the brothers do exist.
Furthermore, the fields and lands belonging to the brothers do exist.
The eldest brother is well-pleased;
the elder brothers are well-pleased.
Thus ends the fourteenth lesson.
The masculine noun ending in the vowel *ū* is called the word *abhibhū*. [Examples:
"The Tathāgata Abhibhū gave a Dhamma teaching";
"The Tathāgatas Abhibhū gave Dhamma teachings."
O Conqueror, Tathāgata, teach the Dhamma!
O Conquerors, Tathāgatas, teach the Dhamma!
I bow my head in homage to the Conqueror, the Tathāgata.
We bow our heads in homage to the Tathāgatas who are Victors;
the Dhamma was taught by the Tathāgata who is the Victor;
the Dhammas were taught by the Tathāgatas who are the Victors.
By the Tathāgata, the Conqueror, the sages have been made happy;
by the Tathāgatas, the Conquerors, the worlds have been made happy.
One offers flowers to the Tathāgata, the Conqueror.
They offer flowers to the Tathāgatas who have overcome [all defilements];
from the Tathāgata who has overcome [all defilements], radiance issues forth;
from the Tathāgatas who have overcome [all defilements], radiances issue forth.
I bow at the feet of the Tathāgata Abhibhū;
I bow at the feet of the Tathāgatas who are Abhibhūs;
my mind delights in the Tathāgata Abhibhū.
The mind is established upon the Tathāgatas who are the conquerors.
Thus ends the fifteenth lesson.
The word *sabbaññu* (omniscient), ending in the vowel *ū*, is said to be masculine.
The Omniscient One, Lord of the World, teaches the Dhamma;
the Omniscient Ones, Lords of the World, teach the Dhamma;
O Omniscient One, Lord of the World, please teach the Dhamma!
O All-Knowing One, Lord of the World, teach the Dhamma!
The great multitude beholds the All-Knowing Lord of the World;
the great multitude beholds the All-Knowing Lord of the World.
The Dhamma is taught by the All-Knowing Lord of the World;
the Dhamma has been taught by the All-Knowing Lords of the World;
through the All-Knowing Lord of the World, beings go to the state of peace.
By the All-Knowing Lords of the World, the worlds have been made happy;
I renounce my life for the All-Knowing Lord of the World;
I renounce my life for the All-Knowing Lords of the World.
May I attain the state of peace from the All-Knowing Lord of the World;
may they attain the state of peace from the All-Knowing Lords of the World;
I pay homage at the feet of the All-Knowing Lord of the World.
We pay homage at the feet of the All-Knowing Lords of the World;
the world places its trust in the All-Knowing Lord of the World;
the worlds place their trust in the All-Knowing Lords of the World.
Thus ends the sixteenth lesson.
The masculine noun *go* ending in the vowel *o* is now explained.
A bull (*usabha*) goes straight.
The cows and bulls walk straight;
O bull among men, walk straight!
The cowherd drives the cattle into the pen.
The cowherds block the cows in the pen;
by means of one ox, a cart is brought;
by means of oxen, carts are brought.
The cow-owner makes his living by means of the cow;
the cow-owners make their living by means of cows;
the cowherd gives grass to the cow.
The cowherds give grass to the cows;
fear arises from the bull for the cows;
fears are produced by the bulls because of the cows.
The quality of a bull is white;
the qualities of bulls are the measure.
When the bull is present, the owner of the cattle is pleased.
Cowherds take pleasure in bulls and oxen.
Thus ends the seventeenth lesson.
Thus ends [the section] on masculine nouns in the *Padamañjarī*.
The First Chapter.
Now, the feminine noun *kaññā* ending in *-ā* is explained.
A maiden causes a female servant to perform work.
The young women made the slave-girl perform work, saying:
"O girl, you too should do what is wholesome;
O young women, you all should do what is wholesome."
The mother causes the daughter to perform wholesome deeds;
the mother and father cause the daughters to perform wholesome deeds;
even sesame seeds are roasted for the daughter.
Grains are roasted by means of young women;
some men behave well toward a single young woman;
some men behave well toward many young women.
A man gives ornaments to a maiden;
a man gives ornaments to maidens;
no man departs from a maiden.
Some men consort with maidens;
there are garments and ornaments for the maiden,
and there are also garments and ornaments for the maidens.
A certain man has confidence in a girl;
certain girls have confidence in a man.
Thus is the first reading.
The feminine noun *ratti* is said to end in the vowel *i*.
The night shines beautifully with moonlight;
the nights shine beautifully with moonlight.
O night, shine forth with moonlight!
O nights, shine forth with moonlight!
Without looking about at night, I shall listen to the Dhamma.
We listen to the Dhamma without looking at the nights;
whatever path is obstructed by night,
and whatever paths are obstructed by nights.
By night the chief of thieves steals;
by nights the chief of thieves steal.
At the time of light, one gives a lamp for the sake of light.
They give lamps as a light for the nights at the time of darkness;
they are not abstaining from food at night;
they are not abstaining from eating at improper times.
There is thick darkness during the night;
there are nights of thick darkness;
the sun does not appear during the night.
At night, they seize their prey with hissing sounds.
Thus is the second reading.
The word *nadī* is said to be a feminine noun ending in the vowel *ī*.
The river flows with uninterrupted continuity;
the rivers flow with uninterrupted continuity.
O river of uninterrupted continuity, give water!
O river, you who flow in an uninterrupted stream, give us water!
He sees the river as flowing in an uninterrupted stream;
he sees rivers as flowing in uninterrupted streams.
The water of the river is constantly carried away;
by the rivers the water is constantly carried away;
the farmer sows his field along the river.
Farmers sow their fields with rivers;
some fools give poison to the rivers,
and some fools cause the rivers themselves to become poisonous.
From the river flow the small streams,
and from the river indeed arises the great flood; such is the great flood of rivers.
Furthermore, a multitude of fish roams in the river;
in rivers, fish, turtles, and so forth roam.
Thus is the third reading.
The word *yāgu* is said to be a feminine noun ending in the vowel *u*.
*Yāgu paccate yaññadattena* (rice gruel is being cooked by Yajñadatta).
*Yāguyo paccante yaññadattehi* (rice gruels are being cooked by the Yajñadattas).
"O gruel, you indeed speak of hunger;
O gruels, you all speak of hunger.
Any person whatsoever drinks the gruel."
Whosoever people drink gruel,
their digestive fire is destroyed; indeed, by means of gruels, the digestive fires are destroyed.
A certain disease is pacified by rice-gruel;
some diseases are pacified by rice-gruels;
furthermore, the cook provides salt for the rice-gruel.
The cooks give salt to the rice gruels;
indeed, the smoke of the rice gruel departs;
indeed, the smokes of the rice gruels depart.
There exists heat in rice gruel;
there exist heats in rice gruels.
Furthermore, grains of rice are present in the rice gruel.
But in the case of *yāgu*, there are grains (*sittāni*).
Thus is the fourth reading.
The word *mātṛ* (mother), ending in the vowel *u* and being feminine in gender, is now stated.
The mother feeds the son food;
the mothers feed the sons food;
O mother, may you live long!
O mothers, may you live long!
The son and his offspring nourish the mother;
even the sons and their offspring nourish the mother.
The son is made to eat food by the mother;
the son was made to eat food by the mothers;
the son also attains happiness through the mother.
Sons also attain happiness through their mothers;
sons give food to their mother,
and sons also give garments to their mothers.
A son disappears from his mother; sons disappear from their mothers;
moreover, a mother may have many sons.
Mothers have many sons, yet the mother delights in the son born of her own body;
among all those who are sons to mothers, she delights in him.
Thus ends the fifth lesson.
The word *jambu*, ending in the vowel *ū* and belonging to the feminine gender, is now explained.
Furthermore, the *jambu* tree was experienced by the Tathāgata.
"O Jambu, those [treasures] were enjoyed by the Tathāgatas;
O Jambu, give even the gold of Jambu!
O Jambus, give even the gold of Jambu!"
Anyone at all sees the Jambu tree;
those who see it see the Jambu tree,
yet the digestive fire within the Jambu tree is struck back.
But when the digestive fire strikes the Jambu tree,
whoever among those on the Jambu tree lives,
and whosoever among those on the Jambu trees live—
But whoever praises Jambudvīpa,
the great multitude indeed praises it; for from Jambudvīpa,
indeed, the gold of Jambunada is born.
From the Jambu tree, indeed, gold from the Jambu river arises;
the Jambu fruits have a sweet flavor,
and the Jambu fruits have a sweet flavor.
Furthermore, there is gold from the Jambu River in Jambudīpa;
indeed, gold from the Jambu River exists in Jambudīpa.
Thus is the sixth reading.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Padamañjarī*, concerning nouns in the feminine gender.
Now, the word *citta*, which is a neuter noun ending in the vowel *a*, is explained.
The mind cognizes its own continuum; minds cognize their own beings.
O mind, cognize your own continuum!
O minds, recognize your own continuum!
Whosoever are the people who will restrain their minds,
they will restrain all minds.
By the mind all people are led;
by the minds all people are led;
by the mind the man of pride is defiled.
Some person here purifies the mind;
some person gives instruction on the mind;
and some persons give instruction on minds.
The object arises from the mind; objects arise from minds;
they have come under the sway of the mind, which is subject to impermanence.
A reflection arose in their minds:
"When the mind is unprotected, bodily action is unprotected;
when the mind is guarded, bodily action is protected."
Thus ends the first reading.
Now, the word *mana* is stated as a neuter noun ending in *a*.
It conceives (*maññati*) its own continuum as "self" (*attano*).
They conceive themselves as "mine," O mind;
conceive your own continuity as "I," O mind;
conceive your own continuity as "ours," O minds.
Having gladdened the mind, I shall go to heaven;
having gladdened the mind, we shall go to heaven.
By means of the mind, wholesome and unwholesome karma is performed.
Wholesome and unwholesome kamma has been performed by means of the mind;
the practitioner of yoga cognizes phenomena by means of the mind;
practitioners of yoga cognize phenomena by means of the mind.
One gives counsel to a corrupted mind;
they give counsel to corrupted minds;
and by means of the mind, an object arises.
Objects arise for the mind;
one who has fallen under the power of the mind’s impermanent nature,
a reflection then arose in his mind.
When the mind is unprotected, bodily action is unprotected;
when the mind is guarded, bodily action is protected.
Thus is the second reading.
The word *guṇavantu* is said to be a neuter noun ending in the vowel *a*.
Thus: *guṇavaṃ kulaṃ puññaṃ karoti* (the virtuous family performs merit), and *guṇavantāni kulāni puññaṃ karonti* (virtuous families perform merit).
O virtuous one, let your family perform merit;
O virtuous ones, let your families perform merit.
Anyone who sees a virtuous person [sees merit].
Whoever sees families that possess virtue,
a monastery has been built by a virtuous family,
or monasteries have been built by families possessing virtue.
The world fares well through families possessed of virtue;
through families possessed of virtue, the worlds fare well.
The wealthy man bestows wealth upon the family that possesses virtue.
The wealthy give their wealth to families possessed of virtue;
from a virtuous family, no one at all departs;
and from families possessed of virtue, no one whatsoever departs.
There is a reputation for virtue in a family of the virtuous;
there is a reputation for virtue in families of those who possess virtue;
my mind also delights in a family that possesses virtue.
The mind is established upon families possessing virtues.
Thus is the third reading.
Now, the word *gacchanta* is stated as a neuter noun ending in the vowel *a*.
The virtuous one going goes to beautiful Nibbāna;
those going who possess virtue go to Nibbāna.
O virtuous one, you too, while going, shall go to a happy destination.
O virtuous ones who are going, may you go to a happy destination.
One person sees a virtuous one going;
another person sees virtuous ones going.
As one who possesses virtue walks, the fragrance of their qualities is wafted abroad;
as those who possess virtue walk, they gather flowers along the way;
as one who possesses virtue walks, the world fares well.
Those who go forth possessing virtuous qualities attain happiness;
people follow those who go forth possessing virtuous qualities;
people welcome those who go forth possessing virtuous qualities.
Some depart from the virtuous while they are departing;
some depart along with the virtuous as they depart;
and the mother and father of the virtuous one depart as he departs.
The name, clan, and so forth of those virtuous ones who are departing;
my mind delights in the virtuous ones as they depart;
my mind is established upon the virtuous ones as they depart.
Thus ends the fourth lesson.
Now the neuter noun *aṭṭhi* (bone), ending in the vowel *i*, is explained.
The bone, the skeleton, and the body are repulsive.
"Bones heaped together are repulsive, friend;
see this skeleton as impermanent. Friend, see these white bones as impermanent."
One sees a bone, along with its flesh and blood, as foul;
one sees heaps of bones as impermanent;
and whatever form is fashioned by means of a body of bones—[one sees that too as such].
Whatever form is fashioned from bones as a body,
by means of the sign of the bone a bhikkhu develops the path;
by means of signs of bones bhikkhus develop the path.
Some give instruction on the body of bones;
some give instruction on bodies of bones;
the practitioner emerges from the body of bones.
Practitioners of yoga proceed by means of bone-bodies:

Indeed, O Great Kings, because of these [other] Great Kings, the great multitude lives happily;
the great multitude gives gifts to that Great King;
the great multitude gives gifts to those Great Kings.
Great fear arises from that great king;
great fears arise from those great kings; and for that great king, there is the auspicious ceremony of sowing.
The great kings have the auspicious rites of sowing;
indeed, the great multitude places its confidence in this great king,
and the great multitude places its confidence in those great kings.
Thus ends the twenty-second lesson.
Now the feminine gender forms are being stated.
Furthermore, that female lay follower listens to the Dhamma with due respect.
This female lay follower listens to the Dhamma respectfully;
this faithful one causes that female lay follower to perform meritorious deeds;
this faithful one causes those female lay followers to perform meritorious deeds.
A bhikkhu is being fed a meal by this female lay follower;
the Saṅgha has been fed a meal by these female lay followers;
or anyone at all is behaving well toward this female lay follower.
Furthermore, those who practice well among these female lay followers give gifts to this female lay follower;
those who are true persons give gifts to these female lay followers.
Whatever anyone enters into by means of this female lay follower (upāsikā),
or whatever anyone enters into by means of these female lay followers; moreover,
this female lay follower has many sons.
The assembly of female lay followers of Amūsā was also large;
anyone who has confidence in this female lay follower Amūsā,
or anyone who has confidence in those female lay followers [is likewise included].
Thus ends the twenty-third lesson.
The forms of the neuter gender are now stated:
That wealthy man constantly produces much merit.
These wealthy ones generate much merit;
that wealthy one causes merit to be performed through faith;
these wealthy ones cause merit to be performed through faith.
By this wealthy man, the bhikkhu was caused to eat a meal;
by these wealthy men, the bhikkhu was caused to eat a meal;
by this wealthy man, even the great multitude has become happy.
By means of these riches, even the great multitude has become happy;
they hold the golden parasol over this wealthy one,
and some would attend upon these wealthy ones.
One might receive gain and honor from that wealthy person;
one might receive gains and honors from those wealthy people;
that wealthy person has a great retinue.
There exist those who are wealthy and possess great retinues;
whoever has faith in this wealthy person,
or whoever has faith in these wealthy people.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth lesson.
The masculine forms are now being stated:
What wise person in this world would ever come under the sway of anger?
Having abandoned the human body, whom have they reached through divine yoga?
For whose sake, friend, did you go forth into homelessness?
And having performed what merits have some gone to the triple heaven?
By whom was this being fashioned? Where is the maker of the being?
By whom was this puppet fashioned? And where indeed is the maker of the puppet?
By whom is your complexion such as it is? By whom do you prosper here?
By what meritorious deeds do deities protect me?
By delighting in whom is a being liberated from all suffering?
And for whom does merit always increase, both by day and by night?
Why did you not lament in such great terror?
By which noble ones indeed was this common person distinguished?
Having understood whose Dhamma, did you utter such speech?
"Having understood what Dhamma did they sever the bond of existence?
At what time, O Hero, was the supreme enlightenment aspired to by you?
And among which lineages of disciples, O Lord of Sages, were they fully satisfied?"
Thus ends the twenty-fifth lesson.
The feminine gender forms are now being stated.
And who gave this gift of a well-made couch, chairs, and so forth?
Having performed various kinds of merit, Kāyā went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
What meditation did she cultivate, and what virtue did she maintain?
Who were the female slaves that her husband employed for his work?
By what means does a female lay follower always hear the Dhamma?
And by what virtuous women does she always hear the Dhamma?
By what knowledge does my son attain this happiness?
By which trainings do my sons attain this happiness?
To which female lay follower should a wealthy man give a gift,
and to which female lay follower should a virtuous man give a gift?
From what body of water do all small streams originate?
And from which rivers do the great rivers originate?
And from which Ganges does the great flood always arise?
Of what kind are the ornaments of maidens?
In which river do fish always wander constantly?
In which Gaṅgās do fish always wander constantly?
Thus ends the twenty-sixth lesson.
The forms of the neuter gender are now stated:
"O dull-witted one, what use have you for matted hair? What use have you for a deerskin garment?"
What kinds of thoughts arise, and how may we know them?
Having seen what mastery over yourself, would you give this wealth to me?
Having performed what meritorious deeds have so many gone to the third heaven?
By what is the world led? By what is it dragged along?
By what is the end of my meritorious deeds not seen?
Why are you dejected, dear father? For whom do you grieve?
With certain flowers, the faithful one reverently makes an offering to Gotama.
With whom should he establish friendship? The Buddhas call that "conduct";
for whom is this supreme gift intended, and to whom should it always be given with respect?
"Why have you become a thief for me?"—thus the King questioned him.
"By what names and by what causes are these people born?
Having understood whose Dhamma, did they sever the bond of existence?"
"Amidst whom does he shine like the moon in the midst of the sky?
With whom am I angry that my friends are displeased with me— I see no misdeed of mine—
and with whom is he, their friend, associating them in meritorious deeds, thinking, 'He is a friend for their welfare'?"
Thus ends the twenty-seventh lesson.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on all nouns in the *Padamañjarī*.
Now, the forms without the suffix -tumha- are stated:
"But you, a man, perform merit" (tvaṃ pana puriso puññaṃ karohi);
"you, men, perform merit" (tumhe purisā puññaṃ karotha).
But you cause a man to perform merit;
you cause men to perform meritorious deeds;
by you, a man, rice is cooked.
While you men are cooking rice,
one man lives by means of you;
some men live by means of you.
The wealthy man gives wealth to you, the man;
the wealthy man gives wealth to you, the men.
Whoever it may be, he takes it away from you, the man.
Whatever names, clans, and so forth belong to you men,
those are the possessions of you men.
"Someone has faith in that man;
some have faith in you, O men.
Thus is the first reading.
"You, woman, go after eating rice;
you women, go after eating rice;
you, woman, cause a man to perform merit."
You women perform meritorious deeds; men [also do so].
Grain is roasted by you women as well;
grain is roasted by you women.
Someone experiences suffering because of that woman;
you ladies experience happiness because of her, Master;
he gives an ornament to your woman, Master.
He gives ornaments for you women, O Master;
he departs from that woman,
and those who depart from you women.
You, woman, have many sons;
you possess garments and ornaments for yourselves, women;
yet, your mind is fixed upon you alone.
But among you women, [the mind] is established upon agreeable things.
Thus is the second reading.
Furthermore, O mind, you contemplate the object.
"Whosoever among you contemplate mental objects with the mind,
and whosoever among you restrain the mind,
they shall restrain their minds."
The fruit of karma was experienced by you through that mind;
the fruit of karma was experienced by you all through those minds.
A person of integrity remembers the Buddha through that mind.
Noble persons remember the Buddha with their own minds;
no one gives instruction to your mind,
yet some give instruction to your minds.
Indeed, fear arises from one's own mind; fears arise from your minds;
a reflection arose in your mind.
A reflection arose in your minds;
indeed, in that mind of yours a wholesome state of mind was established,
and in your minds wholesome states of mind were established.
Thus is the third reading:
"I, though a man, perform merit;
we, moreover, being men, perform merit."
He causes me, a person, to perform merit;
he causes us, persons, to perform meritorious deeds;
by me, a person, the fruit of karma has been experienced.
The fruit of karma has been experienced by us men;
some have been well-conducted by me as a man,
and some have been well-conducted by us men.
The wealthy man gives wealth to us men;
the one who possesses fruit gives fruit to us men;
some depart from me, a man.
Fears arise for us because of men;
there is the name, clan, and so forth of our man,
and there is the possession of our men.
"Whoever has faith in me as a man—
someone among us men who is most gentle.
Thus is the fourth recitation.
"I, a maiden, perform merit;
we, maidens, perform meritorious deeds;
he causes me, a maiden, to perform merit."
He causes the girls to perform merit;
rice is cooked by me, the girl;
rice is cooked by us, the girls.
Happiness and suffering reach the girl through me;
happiness and suffering reach us, the girls, [through her];
he gives an ornament to our girl.
"He gives ornaments to our daughters;
therefore, this girl is inferior to my daughter,
and this girl is superior to us [other] girls."
The clothes and ornaments belong to my daughter;
she is the possession of us;
my mind does not rest upon this daughter of mine.
"My mind is fixed upon the maidens among us.
Thus is the fifth recitation.
But you, Citta, should discern the object.
"We shall know the mind and its object;
some will restrain my mind, and some will restrain our minds."
By my mind the fruit of karma has been experienced;
by our minds the fruit of karma has been experienced.
By my mind, the noble person recollects the Buddha.
With our own minds we remember the Buddha;
someone gives me instruction for my mind,
while others give instructions for our minds.
But fear arises from my own mind; fears arise from our minds.
This reflection arose in my mind.
A reflection arose in our minds:
"In my mind, a wholesome state of mind has been established;
in our minds, wholesome states of mind have been established."
Thus ends the sixth recitation.
"But you may go to the village; we, however, shall not go to the village."
"Monks, having abandoned you, I shall depart;
let us not quarrel today.
But what indeed was that deed of yours?"
But what indeed is that action of mine?
And what indeed is wholesome action for you?
And what indeed is unwholesome action?
"I shall give you five excellent villages;
you too must give me one excellent village.
Monks, I shall teach the Dhamma to you."
"Share with us the sovereignty;
however, let your head be like that of a human being.
And as for my wealth, Sakka, it is abundant."
"I am pleased that the Teacher, our Blessed One, has arrived while you were in such a state of mind;
for from those words, 'These forms are not ours,' each word by word,"
Therefore, those [words] have not been stated by me in the lists of nouns (*nāmikapantī*).
The particle *vo* and *no* occur in the senses of the nominative (*paccatte*), the accusative (*upayoge*), the instrumental (*karaṇe*),
the dative (*sampadāniye*), and in the expression of possession (*sāmissa vacane*).
"It occurs in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa), the recipient (sampadāna), and the sense of ownership (sāmī);
it should be understood by the wise who see the method as 'this is my word'.
Thus ends the seventh lesson.
Thus ends the fifth chapter on pronouns lacking gender in the *Padamañjarī*.
Herein, the masculine forms are stated.
Two Great Kings rule the kingdom;
he approaches both Great Kings;
a battle was fought with the two Great Kings.
By two Great Kings the inhabitants of the realm live;
they present offerings to the two Great Kings;
and from the two Great Kings dangers arise.
It is the possession of two great kings;
the minds of the two great kings are established therein.
These are called the forms of feminine characteristics.
Two maidens perform meritorious deeds;
two maidens cause meritorious deeds to be performed;
meritorious deeds have been performed by the two maidens.
Through two daughters one experiences pleasure and pain;
one gives ornaments to two daughters;
between these two daughters, this daughter is superior.
There is clothing and ornament for two maidens;
the minds of the two maidens are established upon these.
These are called neuter gender forms.
Two families perform deeds of merit such as giving;
two families cause deeds of merit such as giving to be performed;
the Saṅgha was fed by two families.
The Saṅgha attains happiness through two families;
some perform honor for these two families;
through these two families, a certain person departs.
"The names, clans, and so forth of two families;
my mind is established in these two families.
Thus is the first reading.
These are called masculine forms. For example:
"Three men are building a monastery," or "A certain person approaches three men."
A monastery was caused to be built by three men;
those who live by means of these three men, whoever they may be,
are wealthy men who give wealth to these three men.
Dangers arise from three kinds of men;
there is possession by three kinds of men;
one may place confidence in any of these three kinds of men.
These are called the forms of female characteristics.
Three women perform meritorious deeds;
three women cause meritorious deeds to be performed.
The Saṅgha was fed by three women;
a certain man lives off three women;
he gives ornaments to the three women.
A certain man departs from three women;
a certain man becomes the ornaments for three women;
a certain man places his trust in three women.
These are called the forms of the neuter gender.
Three families perform meritorious deeds;
three families cause meritorious deeds to be performed.
Meritorious deeds are performed by three kinds of families;
those who live by means of three kinds of families are the wealthy ones who give wealth to these three families.
Fears do not arise from three families;
one person has great wealth in three families and places his confidence in those three families.
Thus ends the second reading.
These masculine forms are now being stated.
The Four Great Kings exercise sovereignty.
One approaches the four Great Kings;
by the four Great Kings merits are performed,
and by the four Great Kings do the great masses of people live.
They present a gift for the Four Great Kings;
fears arise from the Four Great Kings;
it is the ornament of the Four Great Kings.
The great multitude places its faith in the Four Great Kings.
These are called the forms of feminine characteristics.
The four maidens perform meritorious deeds.
Four maidens cause meritorious deeds to be performed;
by four maidens the Saṅgha is fed a meal;
by four maidens men meet their death.
They give ornaments to four maidens;
this maiden is superior to the four maidens;
she possesses the ornament of the four maidens.
A certain man places his confidence in four maidens.
These are called neuter gender forms.
Four clans perform much merit.
Some men belong to four families;
some have a monastery built by four families;
some live on the support of four families.
They perform honors for the four families;
some enter among the four families;
"four families" refers to names, clans, and so forth.
The great multitude has faith in the four families.
Thus is the third reading.
The five great elements remain.
One sees the five great elements;
one acts well by means of the five great elements;
one is fashioned by the five great elements.
It is given to the five great elements;
it departs by means of the five great elements;
it belongs to the five great elements.
Established upon the five great elements (mahābhūta),
the three gender-forms (liṅgarūpa) are spoken of;
however, the five great elements themselves remain [as their basis].
There are five masters of the bases of mastery;
furthermore, there are five types of persons;
furthermore, there are five stages.
Furthermore, five women stand;
the five great elements stand;
five consciousnesses arise.
In this manner, it should be applied in all instances.
Thus ends the fourth reading.
Now, the forms of the three genders are being stated.
The six great elements remain,
yet one sees the six conquerors;
the deed was performed by six men.
One person is pleasing to the six grounds;
another departs with six maidens;
yet another belongs to the possession of the six beings.
Furthermore, it is established within the six types of consciousness.
The three gender-forms are now being discussed;
however, the seven great elements remain present.
One sees seven conquerors;
karma was performed by seven men;
someone finds pleasure in the seven stages.
A certain person departs with seven maidens;
it belongs to the seven elements and is established within the seven consciousnesses.
Thus ends the fifth lesson.
The forms of the three genders are now stated.
Furthermore, the eight great elements (mahābhūta) remain.
One sees eight conquerors;
work has been done by eight men;
someone is pleasing to eight grounds.
Someone departs with eight maidens;
it belongs to the eight elements,
yet it is established within the eight consciousnesses.
The forms of the Tiliṅga are said [to be these].
However, the nine great elements remain;
one sees the nine conquerors.
Some have their work done by nine men;
some find pleasure in nine levels;
some depart with nine maidens.
It belongs to the nine beings,
yet it is established in the nine consciousnesses.
Thus ends the sixth reading.
The forms of the Tiliṅga are thus called.
But the ten great elements remain;
the ten masters see them.
One person has his karma performed by ten men;
another finds pleasure among ten living beings;
yet another departs with ten maidens.
It belongs to the ten beings,
yet it is established in ten types of consciousness.
The three gender-forms are now explained.
The eleven great elements abide; the twelve masters abide;
and the thirteen persons indeed abide.
There are fourteen stages;
fifteen maidens stand there;
and sixteen elements stand there.
Seventeen types of consciousness arise.
Three types of gender-forms (liṅga-rūpa) are spoken of.
Furthermore, the eighteen great primary elements (mahābhūta) persist.
One who has mastered the eighteen [bases] sees;
the deed was performed by eighteen men;
it is pleasing to the eighteen grounds.
Someone departs accompanied by eighteen maidens;
it belongs to eighteen beings and is established within eighteen states of consciousness.
Thus ends the seventh lesson.
Thus concludes the sixth chapter of the *Padamañjarī*, concerning the names of the plural number.
Now, the forms of the three genders are being stated.
“Ekūnavīsati,” “ekūnavīsaṃ,” and so forth;
likewise, “ekūnavīsāya,” “ekūnavīsāyaṃ,” and “ekūnavīsati bhikkhūpi tiṭṭhanti.”
He saw nineteen monks;
the Dhamma was taught by nineteen monks;
a formal act was performed by nineteen maidens.
One performs an action with nineteen states of consciousness;
one gives robes to nineteen monks;
one gives wealth to nineteen maidens.
But among nineteen types of minds, it is pleasing;
for some, it departs with nineteen monks;
for some, it departs with nineteen maidens.
Someone departs with nineteen minds;
[he takes] what belongs to nineteen monks;
[he takes] what belongs to nineteen maidens.
The property of nineteen minds,
established among nineteen monks,
and established among nineteen maidens.
It is established among the nineteen types of consciousness.
Thus ends the first reading:
Masculine forms.
Nineteen monks also stand;
he sees nineteen monks;
[the Dhamma] was taught by nineteen monks.
It was established among nineteen monks.
There were the forms of female characteristics. Nineteen maidens stood there.
He sees nineteen maidens;
the work was performed by nineteen maidens;
it is established among nineteen maidens.
The forms of the neuter gender.
Nineteen consciousnesses arise;
one sees nineteen consciousnesses.
Action performed by nineteen types of consciousness is established in nineteen types of consciousness.
Thus is the second reading.
Masculine forms:
"Twenty monks stand," "He sees twenty monks."
Taught by twenty monks,
established among twenty monks:
these are the forms of the female gender.
Twenty maidens are standing there;
he sees twenty maidens;
the work was performed by twenty maidens.
Established among the twenty maidens are the forms of the neuter gender;
twenty consciousnesses arise.
One sees twenty states of consciousness;
karma was performed by twenty states of consciousness;
it is established within twenty states of consciousness.
Vīsaṃ, vīsaṃ, vīsāya, vīsāyaṃ;
likewise ekavīsa, dvāvīsa,
bāvīsa, tevīsa, catuvīsa, and so forth.
Thus ends the third reading.
Masculine forms:
"Thirty monks stand."
He sees thirty monks;
it was taught by thirty monks;
it is established among thirty monks.
The forms of female gender.
Thirty maidens stand there;
he sees thirty maidens as well.
The grammatical operation is performed by thirty feminine forms;
it is established among the thirty feminine forms.
These are the neuter gender forms.
Thirty consciousnesses arise;
he sees thirty consciousnesses;
karma is performed by means of thirty consciousnesses.
It is established among the thirty types of consciousness.
Thus ends the fourth reading.
Masculine forms.
Forty bhikkhus stand;
he sees forty bhikkhus;
it was taught by forty bhikkhus.
It was established among forty bhikkhus.
There were forms with female characteristics.
Forty maidens also stood there.
He sees it in forty maidens;
the action was performed by forty maidens;
it is established in forty maidens.
The forms of the neuter gender.
Forty types of consciousness also arise;
forty types of consciousness also see.
Kamma performed by forty-four types of consciousness is established within those same forty-four types of consciousness.
"Forty" and so forth are also used.
Thus ends the fifth lesson.
Masculine forms:
"By means of wisdom, O monks, they stand firm."
O monks, he sees with wisdom;
it is taught by monks through wisdom;
it is established among monks through wisdom.
The forms of feminine gender;
through wisdom they stand even as maidens,
and through wisdom they see even as maidens.
The action was performed by fifty maidens;
it is established among fifty maidens.
These are neuter gender forms.
Fifty types of consciousness arise;
he sees fifty types of consciousness;
karma was performed by means of fifty types of consciousness.
It is established in fifty minds.
Likewise, fifty and fifty,
in each set of fifty.
Thus ends the sixth lesson.
Masculine forms.
Sixty monks also remain.
He sees sixty monks;
it was taught by sixty monks;
it is established among sixty monks.
Forms with female characteristics;
sixty maidens stand there,
and he sees sixty maidens.
The neuter gender forms are those for which the grammatical operation is performed by sixty [rules] and which are established among the sixty [forms].
Sixty types of consciousness arise;
one sees sixty types of consciousness;
karma has been performed by means of sixty types of consciousness.
It is established among the sixty types of consciousness.
Thus ends the seventh lesson:
Masculine Nouns.
"Seventy monks, O bhikkhus, remain;
seventy monks, O bhikkhus, one sees;
[the Dhamma] was taught by seventy monks."
Seventy were established among the monks;
seventy maidens remained in female forms.
He sees it even in seventy maidens;
the deed was done by seventy maidens,
and it is established in seventy maidens.
The forms of the neuter gender.
Seventy states of consciousness arise;
one also sees seventy states of consciousness.
Action performed by seventy-one types of consciousness is established within seventy-one types of consciousness; thus it is said,
"seventy," and so forth.
Thus ends the eighth lesson.
Masculine forms.
Even eighty monks remain, O Bhikkhus.
He sees eighty monks;
it was taught by eighty monks;
it is established among eighty monks.
Forms with female characteristics;
he sees even eighty maidens standing there as eighty maidens.
The grammatical operation is performed by means of eighty feminine forms;
it is established within eighty feminine forms.
These are the neuter gender forms.
Eighty types of consciousness arise;
one sees eighty types of consciousness;
karma has been performed by means of eighty types of consciousness.
It is established among eighty types of consciousness.
Thus ends the ninth lesson:
Masculine Nouns.
Ninety monks, O bhikkhus, remain;
ninety monks, O bhikkhus, one sees;
[the Dhamma] is taught by ninety monks.
Ninety [marks] are established among monks;
ninety marks of female characteristics also exist in a maiden.
He sees ninety maidens;
the deed was done by ninety maidens;
it is established in ninety maidens.
The forms of the neuter gender.
Ninety types of consciousness arise;
one also sees ninety types of consciousness.
Kamma performed with ninety minds is established in ninety minds;
likewise for ninety-one, and so forth.
Thus ends the tenth lesson.
But hundreds of monks indeed remain;
but hundreds of monks indeed remain.
Monks, one sees a hundred; monks, one sees hundreds;
the Dhamma has been taught by a hundred monks.
The Dhamma has been taught by a hundred bhikkhus;
one should give a gift to a hundred bhikkhus;
[many people] should give a gift to a hundred bhikkhus.
Some depart with a hundred monks;
some depart with hundreds of monks;
[some take] the bowls and robes of a hundred monks.
The alms-bowls and robes of the hundred bhikkhus;
the mind of the hundred bhikkhus was established;
the mind of the hundred bhikkhus was established.
In this way, "a thousand thousands" should be joined as ten thousand,
a hundred thousand, and ten hundred thousand.
Here too, this is the same method;
but here is the specific method:
there are indeed a hundred bhikkhus.
There are indeed hundreds of women,
and there are indeed hundreds who are dear;
the same principle applies even to thousands.
Thus ends the eleventh lesson.
By multiplying ten by ten, one hundred is formed.
By multiplying a hundred by ten, one thousand is formed.
Multiplying ten thousand by ten makes one hundred thousand;
that is called a "lakh" (lakkha). Multiplying one hundred thousand by ten makes one million.
Multiplying one million by ten makes a "koṭi."
The meaning is "a hundred times a hundred thousand crores.
A hundred times a hundred thousand pakkoṭis is a *pakoṭi*.
A hundred times a hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is a *koṭippakoṭi*.
One hundred thousand koṭippakoṭis is one nahuta;
one hundred thousand nahutas is one ninnahuta;
one hundred thousand ninnahutas is one akkhobhini.
Another method: one, ten, a hundred,
a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million (dasasatasahassa), ten million (koṭi), a hundred million (pakoṭi),
a billion (koṭippakoṭi), and ten billion (nahuta).
"Ninnahutaṃ akkhohiṇī": thus,
when counted starting from one,
the *akṣauhiṇī* reaches its thirteenth position.
Nine thousand nāgas; for every nāga, a hundred chariots;
for every chariot, a hundred horses; for every horse, a hundred men;
for every man, a hundred maidens; for every maiden, a hundred female attendants. Of whom is this? Of King Sātī.
"This is what is called an *akṣauhiṇī*, as spoken by the former teachers:
the *akṣauhiṇī*, the *bhindu*, the *abbuda*,
the *nirabbuda*, the *ahaha*, the *ababa*, the *aṭaṭa*, and the *sugandhika*."
"Uppalaṃ, kumudaṃ, puṇḣarīkaṃ, and likewise padumaṃ—this is said to be the sequence of the *Kathā* and *Mahākathā* texts, which are incalculable (*asaṃkheyya*).
This is the order in the *Kaccāyana*; it contradicts the *Pāli*."
The sequence of the Pāli should be understood as follows:
Nirabbuda, Ababa, Aṭaṭa, Ahaha, Kumuda, Sugandhika,
Uppala, Puṇḍarīka, and Paduma— thus the Victor has declared.
Thus ends the twelfth lesson.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Padamañjarī* concerning the names of numbers.
The treatise *Padamañjarī* is completed.
May there be success!
